stories.title: SBI secures 10 acres for data centre in Bharat Future City
stories.summary: SBI has been allotted a 10-acre land parcel in Meerkhanpet for its proposed data centre, to be located in Bharat Future City. This allocation follows the resolution of a long-standing land dispute with the state government.
stories.why_it_matters: With the land hurdle removed, one of India's largest banks can move forward on its own captive data centre capacity, reinforcing the trend of major financial institutions insourcing critical infrastructure as India's data centre market accelerates.
stories.content:
The Telangana government has allotted a 10-acre land parcel to the State Bank of India (SBI) in Meerkhanpet for its planned data centre project within Bharat Future City. This development positions Bharat Future City as an emerging hub for AI and data centre infrastructure in India, attracting various significant investments already.Seven acres of the land were provided to SBI in exchange for disputed land at Raidurg, while the bank will purchase the remaining three acres. This resolution concludes a dispute between the state government and SBI concerning nearly five acres of land in Raidurg, clearing the path for the data centre's development.

# SBI secures 10 acres for data centre in Bharat Future City

SBI has been allotted a 10-acre land parcel in Meerkhanpet for its proposed data centre, to be located in Bharat Future City. This allocation follows the resolution of a long-standing land dispute with the state government.

- SBI secures 10 acres in Meerkhanpet for a new data centre.
- Project location is Bharat Future City, an emerging AI and data centre hub.
- Land allocation resolves a prior dispute over five acres at Raidurg.

stories.title: Brazil's President Lula signs ReData data center bill into law
stories.summary: The bill was passed by the Senate in September
stories.why_it_matters: A dedicated legal framework reduces regulatory uncertainty for investors eyeing Latin America's largest data center market, potentially unlocking a wave of new builds as hyperscalers and local players gain clearer rules on operations and incentives.
stories.content:
On Tuesday, September 15, during a ceremony at the Planalto Palace, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) signed Bill 278/2026 into law, establishing the Special Taxation Regime for Data Center Services (aka ReData).

The law creates tax incentives for the establishment of data processing centers in the country, with a focus on facilities dedicated to cloud computing and artificial intelligence.

The bill was approved by the Senate on September 1, without any substantive changes from the version that came from the Chamber of Deputies, where it had been passed in February under urgent procedure, without going through the committees.

The Senate rapporteur, Senator Cid Gomes (PSB), reportedly made only editorial adjustments to prevent the bill from returning to the Chamber of Deputies.

The program provides for the suspension of import duties, the IPI tax, the PIS/Pasep taxes, and the COFINS tax — including those on imports — levied on the purchase, in the domestic or foreign market, of information and communication technology equipment and components intended for data centers.

This benefit may be enjoyed for up to five years and becomes a permanent exemption after obligations are fulfilled.

In the case of the Import Tax, the benefit applies only to products with no equivalent manufactured in Brazil, and the Manaus Free Trade Zone retains specific treatment, with the IPI suspension not applying to certain items produced in the region.

According to government estimates, the tax waiver will total approximately 5.2 billion reais ($1bn) in 2026, with 1 billion reais ($193.7m) projected for each of the following two years. Data from the Ministry of Finance indicate that approximately 60 percent of the data and artificial intelligence resources used in Brazil are processed abroad, a trend attributed, in part, to tax costs.

In contrast, companies registered with ReData will be required to allocate at least 10 percent of their data processing, storage, and handling capacity to the Brazilian market, without the option to export or retain that portion; comply with sustainability criteria, including the use of electricity from renewable or low-emission sources; maintain a Water Efficiency Index of no more than 0.05 liters of water per kilowatt-hour; and invest in the country an amount equivalent to two percent of the value of products purchased using the benefits. Companies located in the North, Northeast, Midwest, or in areas covered by regional development agencies have these requirements reduced to eight percent and 1.6 percent, respectively, and at least 40 percent of investments intended to stimulate the digital economy must be directed to these regions.

Failure to comply with these obligations may result in the collection of suspended taxes, with interest and penalties, and, in the case of the domestic market supply target, the suspension of benefits for new purchases, which will result in the revocation of eligibility if the noncompliance is not corrected within 180 days. Entry into the program will require authorization from the Ministry of Finance, and oversight will be the responsibility of that ministry and the Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade, and Services.

*This piece was translated from DCD's Portuguese site and edited by a member of DCD staff.*

stories.title: Brazil's Eveo plans data center in Recife
stories.summary: Company adding to sites in Fortaleza, São Paulo, and Curitiba
stories.why_it_matters: Eveo's move reflects rising demand for data center capacity outside Brazil's southeast hub, and positions regional enterprises in the northeast with lower-latency local infrastructure as digital adoption spreads beyond the major metros.
stories.content:
Brazilian dedicated server and private cloud provider Eveo is launching a new data center in Recife, a city in the state of Pernambuco.

The facility will reportedly open soon, with plans to reach Tier III levels. Full details on location and specifications haven't been shared.

Eevo has operated a data center in Fortaleza since 2024 and will move into a new facility in Recife in response to high demand in a region that still lacks local infrastructure.

According to the company, the distances in the Northeast - about 800km, or a ten-hour drive, between Recife and Fortaleza - make it impractical to serve the entire region from a single location, especially for latency-sensitive applications.

The company also has facilities in São Paulo (Cotia and Osasco) and Curitiba, and has capacity at a data center in Miami, Florida.

*This piece was translated from DCD's Portuguese site and edited by a member of DCD staff.*

stories.title: DCD Intelligence: Data center expansion is outpacing talent
stories.summary: More than two-thirds report staffing below operational requirements
stories.why_it_matters: Operators face delayed commissioning, heavier overtime burdens, and rising attrition as new capacity comes online faster than engineers and technicians can be hired and trained — a constraint that could slow the very expansion the market is counting on.
stories.content:
Data center expansion is massively outpacing available talent, as the industry strains under the weight of its own growth, according to the results of *DCD Intelligence’s* new workforce survey.

Staffing is stretched thin across all sectors, with more than two-thirds of developers and operators reporting staffing levels below what their operations require. Nearly a third are operating at under 80 percent of demand.

These issues are reflected across all critical areas, where gaps risk reduced performance and increased downtime, the report said, with the shortages most acute in facilities and physical infrastructure, power and cooling systems, and IT operations.

These shortages are largely down to recruitment issues and lack of available talent, with nearly half of respondents to the survey stating that a lack of technical knowledge in prospective hires was the biggest barrier to entry. Respondents also cited low industry awareness as an issue.

The survey also examined how organizations are hiring and where they are sourcing new talent from. Organizations are increasingly looking toward adjacent technical infrastructure and utilities sectors to fill roles, with cross-hires from the telecoms industry falling into third place.

Fluid dynamics and power expertise were the biggest drivers of workforce expansion, with respondents looking to power and water utilities and the oil and gas industry to fill these roles.

Organizations are also looking to expand education-based pathways, including internships, apprenticeship programs, and university programs.

“Looking across these different issues, the one clear thread is that the industry is lacking structure in its recruitment and training processes. Staffing gaps, poor onboarding, inconsistent training, and slow upskilling are all caused by the absence of consistent and deliberate systems for building and sustaining talent,” the report said.

“The organizations best positioned to win out of the industry’s explosive growth are those that treat their workforce development as core infrastructure to their businesses. Investing in deliberately structured training and standardized onboarding are a must, as is upskilling staff on AI and other new technologies coming into use in the industry. Without a shift in this regard, skill gaps and recruitment shortages will continue, and could widen in the coming years as the pace of technological change continues to accelerate.”

stories.title: PGIM sells data center development site in Munich
stories.why_it_matters: The transaction signals active trading of development land in Europe's tighter markets, where ready-to-build data center sites are scarce — and suggests investors are still willing to pay for prime locations despite higher financing costs.
stories.content:
Asset manager PGIM has sold a German data center development site near Munich to an unnamed European infrastructure investor.

Full details on the project, the terms of the deal, and the buyer weren’t shared.

The company said the 30MW development in Greater Munich (Unterschleissheim) comes with a building permit and regulatory approvals.

PGIM’s closed-ended value-add fund European Value Partners (EVP) II acquired the site in 2024.

“The sale of this Munich site crystalizes the value created through securing planning consent and grid connection,” said Nabil Mabed, head of value add Europe, real estate at PGIM. “This deal also underscores our expertise in identifying the right properties in metropolitan areas and transforming them into data-center-ready developments — adding value for our investors, regional businesses, and end-users.”

PGIM is the global asset management business of NYSE-listed Prudential Financial, Inc., with $1.5 trillion in assets under management. The firm’s real estate business is the world’s second-largest real estate investment manager, with $219 billion in assets under management.

PGIM Real Estate has previously partnered with Equinix on a number of hyperscale developments and sold a California site earmarked for data center development to Amazon. The company previously owned a portfolio of US data centers alongside Digital Realty later sold to Menlo Equities. Earlier this year the company bought a development site in Melbourne, Australia.

NTT has a data center in Unterschleißheim that launched in 2017; nLighten, Portus, Equinix, NorthC, and EdgeConneX currently operate data centers around the Munich area.

stories.title: Gazprom partners with Crypto Energy to deploy modular data center at gas field in Siberia - report
stories.summary: The pilot project will utilize gas from a depleted field in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region
stories.why_it_matters: The pilot illustrates how energy producers are using modular data centers to convert otherwise unmarketable gas into computing revenue — a model that could spread among remote energy assets and reshape where energy-intensive compute gets sited.
stories.content:
Russian state-owned gas company Gazprom has launched a pilot project with cryptocurrency firm Crypto Energy to power a modular data center site behind the meter using natural gas.

The project will be located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region, in northwestern Siberia. According to local reports, the modular data center will utilize gas from the depleted Medvezhye gas field.

"Residual reserves of depleted fields in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug are becoming a profitable resource base for prospective data centers. Due to low reservoir pressure, it's more rational to use such reserves near production sites for energy-intensive data processing facilities," the companies said in a statement.

According to the partners, Crypto Energy will construct the modular data center and a gas piston power plant, which will directly power it. Gazprom will in turn provide low-pressure gas to the facility, with the local regional government assisting computing capacity owners in obtaining government support.

"In addition to using low-pressure gas, Gazprom's project portfolio includes providing its own spare power generation capacity at fields for the creation of data centers in Russian regions. Specifically, such a project has been implemented at the Bovanenkovo field," Gazprom added.

The project comes shortly after the Russian government banned Bitcoin mining in Moscow and the surrounding region to ease pressure on the country’s ailing power grid.

At present, cryptocurrency mining reportedly consumes approximately 1GW of power in Moscow alone, with projections of up to 3.6GW by 2032, representing 17 percent of peak electricity demand for the entire grid.

The ban did not impact cryptocurrency mining in the Siberian and eastern territories, where the cost of energy is significantly cheaper, with the Gazprom project as evidence of this.

stories.title: Russia claims strikes on De Novo data center in Kyiv, Ukraine
stories.summary: Strikes were part of a wider infrastructure attack
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on data centers raise the stakes for cloud and hosting resilience in Ukraine, potentially accelerating data migration abroad and increasing demand for redundant, geographically distributed capacity among Ukrainian enterprises and their providers.
stories.content:
Russia claims to have struck the De Novo data center in Kyiv, Ukraine, one of the country’s largest data centers.

According to Russian state news agency, TASS, Russian forces launched a number of strikes earlier this week targeting Ukrainian industry and infrastructure, including metallurgical and radio-electronics facilities, defense industry sites, and energy infrastructure.

The attacks took place across Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and the Odesa region.

As part of these attacks, Russian officials claimed to have hit the De Novo data center. TASS said the site supports server equipment for military purposes and processes, transmits, and stores data, including intelligence data, for the Ukrainian army.

De Novo says it is a sovereign cloud and AI provider, operating and supporting mission critical IT systems. According to its website, the data center hosts the country’s largest banks and is the site of the biggest Infrastructure-as-a-Service cloud in Ukraine.

The De Novo data center was built in 2010, with expansion commissioned in 2017.

The site is one of the largest data centers in Ukraine with Tier III compliance, with a capacity of 360 rack spaces. The primary building at the Kyiv site spans 2,117 sqm (22,787 sq ft), with a total power capacity of 3.05MW and 1.05MW of IT power. It also hosts a secondary building across 1,200 sqm (12,916 sq ft) with 500kW of IT power available.

Earlier this year, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian data center facility in Russian-occupied Prymorsk, in the Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine.
